# Fixture corpus — throwaway safes for the cockpit-secrets test suite

Every file in this directory is a **decoy**. None of them holds a real
credential, none of them is derived from a real safe, and every passphrase is
printed below on purpose so the test suite can open them without a human.

> If you are about to add a fixture: it must be generated, it must be
> reproducible from `gen_fixtures.sh`, and it must never be a copy of a real
> database. A "just this once" real safe in a repository is how credentials
> leak, and this directory is the obvious place for it to happen.

---

## The passphrase

```
fixture-pass-do-not-reuse
```

One passphrase for every fixture that needs one. It is also in `manifest.json`,
which is what tests should read — do not hardcode it.

`lab-kdbx41-keyfile-only.kdbx` has **no** passphrase: it opens with its key file
alone, which is exactly the `password_required: false` case in the registry
schema (`docs/CONTRACT.md`).

Sizes and digests are re-measured into `manifest.json` on every
`gen_fixtures.sh --build`; if the table and the manifest disagree, the manifest
is right.

| File | What it is |

| `manifest.json` | machine-readable index: passphrase, key file, size, digest, **provenance** |

| `lab-pws3.spec.json` | the content of the PWS3 fixture, as input to `pws3_oracle write` |
| `attachment-notes.txt` | attachment payload, text (159 bytes) |
| `attachment-blob.bin` | attachment payload, bytes `0x00`–`0xFF` — every byte value, so base64 round-tripping is really tested (256 bytes) |
| `lab-kdbx41-*.keyx` | KeePassXC 2.0 XML key files, generated by `keepassxc-cli` itself, mode `0400` |
| `gen_fixtures.sh` | the generator / re-verifier |
| `kdbx_reformat.py` | writes the empty KDBX 4 headers that `keepassxc-cli merge` then fills |
| `gen_manifest.py` | writes `manifest.json` |

## Provenance — the part that matters

`docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` **I19**: *"a reader and a writer that share a bug
round-trip perfectly and interoperate with nothing."* A fixture is only evidence
if a **foreign** implementation produced it or accepts it. So, honestly, file by
file:

### The KDBX fixtures — foreign, with one seam

Every `.kdbx` in this directory has its final bytes written by
**`keepassxc-cli` 2.7.10**, and every one of them is re-opened by
`keepassxc-cli db-info` + `ls -R -f` + `show -s` before `gen_fixtures.sh` will
report success.

There is one seam, and it is not hidden. Measured on this host:

> **`keepassxc-cli db-create` has no switch for the format version, the cipher
> or the KDF, and always produces KDBX 3.1 with AES-KDF** — including with
> `--decryption-time`, which only changes the round count. `import` behaves the
> same way.

So the 4.x variants are made in three steps:

1. `kdbx_reformat.py` (pykeepass) writes an **empty** database whose header
   carries the cipher and KDF we want. No content, no entries.
2. `keepassxc-cli merge` merges the 3.1 fixture into it. **KeePassXC does the
   merge and writes the file**, preserving the target's cipher and KDF.
3. For the 4.1 fixtures, `keepassxc-cli mv` moves `Moved Entry` from `Staging`
   to `Archive`. That records `PreviousParentGroup`, a KDBX 4.1-only element,
   and KeePassXC then stamps the file as 4.1. This is the only honest way to get
   a 4.1 file out of this toolchain: **KeePassXC always writes the lowest format
   version that can express the database**, so a hand-set minor version is
   overwritten on the next save.

Net position: pykeepass contributed 152 bytes of empty header parameters;
KeePassXC contributed every byte of content, every MAC and the final encoding,
and KeePassXC re-reads all of it. That is a materially stronger claim than
"pykeepass wrote it", and a weaker one than "KeePassXC created it from nothing".
Both halves are stated because I19 is about not overclaiming.

### The PWS3 fixture — the honest gap

`lab-pws3.psafe3` is written by **our own** `tests/oracle/pws3_oracle`, and
there is no foreign implementation on this host to check it against.

`docs/UPSTREAM-REVIEW.md` §1 says Ubuntu's `passwordsafe` 1.22.0 ships
`/usr/bin/pwsafe` and no CLI, and `docs/HOST-FACTS.md` suggests trying
`pwsafe --validate` under `Xvfb`. That was tried. What happened:

| Attempt | Result |
|---|---|
| `pwsafe --help` | exits **0**, lists `-r -v/--validate -e -d -c -s -m -u -h -g --yubi-polling-interval`. So it does accept non-interactive arguments. |
| `xvfb-run -a pwsafe --validate=FILE </dev/null` (45 s) | **timed out, rc 124.** No stdout, no stderr, no exit. |
| `Xvfb :97` + `pwsafe --validate=FILE`, waited 26 s, `xwininfo -root -children` | process alive, **0 child windows mapped**; `xdotool` finds nothing to type into; no output on either stream. |

So `--validate` is not scriptable: it wants a passphrase from a dialog that
never appears headlessly, and there is nothing to drive with `xdotool`. **There
is no `pwsafe`-produced reference fixture in this directory, because this host
cannot produce one.** Saying so is the requirement; implying otherwise would be
bad practice #20 in `docs/UPSTREAM-REVIEW.md` §4.

What partly compensates, and what does not:

* **Does compensate** — `pws3_oracle` is an independent Go implementation
  written from `formatV3.txt` v3.31 alone, using `golang.org/x/crypto/twofish`,
  by an author who had not read `backends/psafe3.py`. Two implementations in two
  languages from one spec disagree where either is wrong; one implementation
  cannot.
* **Does compensate** — the Twofish known-answer vectors. `pws3_oracle vectors`
  checks the published all-zero-key ECB vectors for 128/192/256-bit keys, and
  they match the values `docs/HOST-FACTS.md` measured from Botan 3.10, which is
  what the Python side uses. Three independent Twofish implementations agree
  (Go `x/crypto`, Botan, and Perl `Crypt::Twofish`, all present on this host).
* **Does NOT compensate** — nothing here proves a real Password Safe would open
  this file. That check needs a machine with the GUI and a human, and it remains
  an open item against I19.

## What the content exercises

Both formats carry deliberately parallel content so a test can compare them.

| Thing | KDBX path | PWS3 |
|---|---|---|
| The sentinel | `/Lab/Nested/Router` → Password | record 1, field `0x06` |
| Nested group, two levels | `Lab` → `Nested` | Group field `0x02` = `Lab.Nested` |
| Plain custom field | `Lab Ticket` = `LAB-4711` | — (PWS3 has no custom fields; `0xc0` stands in) |
| Protected custom field | `API Token` | — |
| Attachments | `notes.txt`, `blob.bin` on `Router` | — (attachments are format 0x030F+, not used here) |
| TOTP | `/TOTP Demo` → `otp` attribute | — |
| Non-ASCII everywhere | `/Ünïcødé — 日本語 🔐` | record 2 |
| Expired entry | `/Expiring Account` | record 1 field `0x0a`, in the past |
| Entry tags | `Router` → `fixture,sentinel,lab` | — |
| Zero-length fields | — | record 4 |
| Unknown field types | — | `0x1b` (defined, unimplemented) and `0xc0` (application range, §4.2.1) |
| Multi-block field | — | record 1 Notes, far longer than the 11 bytes that fit in a field's first block |
| Repeated header field | — | `0x11` Empty Group, twice — the only header field §3.2[16] allows to repeat |
| 4.1-only element | `PreviousParentGroup` on `Moved Entry` (4.1 fixtures only) | — |

### The sentinel

```
SENTINEL-DO-NOT-LEAK-8f3a2b
```

Unique across this whole repository. It is the string a leak test greps for in
`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `/proc/<pid>/environ`, the audit log, the job log, and
browser storage (`docs/KNOWN_ISSUES.md` I10, I11, I15). A second sentinel,
`tok-protected-do-not-leak-4c9d1e`, sits in a *protected* custom field, so a
test can tell "the entry listing leaked a password" from "the entry listing
leaked a protected attribute".

### Tree difference between the 4.1 fixtures and the others

The 4.1 fixtures have `Moved Entry` in `/Archive`; the 3.1 and 4.0 fixtures have
it in `/Staging`. That is not an accident — the move is what makes the file 4.1
(see Provenance above). `manifest.json` records both paths as
`moved_entry_41` and `moved_entry_pre41`.

## Rebuilding

```sh
./gen_fixtures.sh                 # verify the committed corpus (default)
./gen_fixtures.sh --build         # build anything missing, then verify
./gen_fixtures.sh --build --force # rebuild everything, then verify
```

`--build` without `--force` will not overwrite an existing fixture: the corpus is
committed, and silently rewriting it would make every fixture-dependent test
unreproducible.

**The KDBX fixtures are not byte-reproducible.** KeePassXC generates fresh
UUIDs, seeds, IVs and timestamps on every run, so `--force` produces different
bytes with the same content, and the digests in `manifest.json` change. That is
inherent, not a defect. **The PWS3 fixture *is* byte-reproducible**:
`pws3_oracle --seed` pins its salt, keys, IV and field padding, so rebuilding it
is a no-op in `git status`. That flag is test-only and the oracle warns loudly
on stderr whenever it is used.

Requirements: `keepassxc-cli` (from `keepassxc-full`), `python3-pykeepass`, and
a built `../oracle/pws3_oracle` (the script builds it if it is missing).

## Rules for anything in this directory

1. No real credential, ever. Not "temporarily", not "for one test".
2. Nothing here is installed. `install.sh` must never copy `tests/`.
3. Never print a fixture's contents from a `/srv/jobs` job — those logs are
   group-readable (`docs/HOST-FACTS.md`), and the sentinel is only a sentinel
   because it is easy to grep for.
4. The `.kdbx` files are mode `0600` and the `.keyx` files `0400`, because
   `backends/base.open_safe_fd` refuses anything with group or other bits set.
   Do not "fix" the permissions.
